title: Deep Batch Active Learning by Diverse, Uncertain Gradient Lower Bounds

elements.name: BADGE: Batch Active learning by Diverse Gradient Embeddings
elements.description: The main proposed algorithm. Starts with M random labeled examples, then iteratively: (1) computes a hallucinated label y_hat for each unlabeled example using the current model, (2) computes gradient embeddings w.r.t. the last layer weights using the hallucinated label, (3) selects a batch by k-MEANS++ seeding on those gradient embeddings, (4) queries labels and retrains.
elements.source_text: BADGE, described in Algorithm 1 starts by drawing an initial set of M examples uniformly at random from U and asking for their labels. It then proceeds iteratively, performing two main computations at each step t: a gradient embedding computation and a sampling computation.
elements.pseudocode:
Require: Neural network f(x; theta), unlabeled pool U, initial count M, iterations T, batch size B.
1: S <- M examples drawn uniformly at random from U with queried labels.
2: Train initial model theta_1 on S by minimizing E_S[CE(f(x;theta), y)].
3: for t = 1, 2, ..., T:
4:   For all x in U \ S:
     (a) Compute hallucinated label y_hat(x) = h_theta_t(x) = argmax_i f(x; theta)_i.
     (b) Compute gradient embedding g_x = d/d(theta_out) CE(f(x;theta), y_hat(x)) at theta=theta_t, where theta_out = last layer parameters.
5:   Use k-MEANS++ seeding on {g_x : x in U \ S} to select B examples as S_t.
6:   S <- S union S_t.
7:   Train model theta_{t+1} on S by minimizing E_S[CE(f(x;theta), y)].
8: end for
9: return Final model theta_{T+1}.

elements.name: k-MEANS++ seeding algorithm
elements.description: The sampling subroutine BADGE uses to select diverse, high-magnitude batches from gradient embeddings. Selects k centroids by iteratively sampling points with probability proportional to their squared distance to the nearest already-chosen centroid.
elements.source_text: Here we briefly review the k-MEANS++ seeding algorithm by (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007). Its basic idea is to perform sequential sampling of k centers, where each new center is sampled from the ground set with probability proportional to the squared distance to its nearest center.
elements.pseudocode:
Require: Ground set G (subset of R^d), target size k.
Ensure: Center set C of size k.

c_1 <- sampled uniformly at random from G.
C_1 <- {c_1}.
for t = 2, ..., k:
  D_t(x) := min_{c in C_{t-1}} ||x - c||_2.
  c_t <- sample x from G with probability D_t(x)^2 / sum_{x in G} D_t(x)^2.
  C_t <- C_{t-1} union {c_t}.
end for
return C_k.

elements.name: Cross-entropy loss
elements.description: The loss function optimized during training. For probabilities p and label y, l_CE(p, y) = ln(1/p_y). This is the loss whose gradient w.r.t. last layer parameters forms the gradient embedding.
elements.source_text: We optimize the parameters by minimizing the cross-entropy loss E_S[l_CE(f(x; theta), y)] over the labeled examples, where l_CE(p, y) = sum_{i=1}^K I(y=i) ln 1/p_i = ln 1/p_y.
elements.pseudocode: l_CE(p, y) = -ln(p_y), where p is the probability vector and y is the label index.

elements.name: Gradient embedding for softmax classification
elements.description: The core computation of BADGE. For the i-th class weight block, the gradient of CE loss w.r.t. W_i when the hallucinated label y_hat is used: (g_x)_i = (p_i - I(y_hat = i)) * z(x; V). This gives a K-d block vector where each block is a scaled version of the penultimate layer output z(x; V).
elements.source_text: Define g_x^y = d/dW l_CE(f(x;theta), y) for a label y and g_x = g_x^{y_hat} as the gradient embedding in our algorithm, where y_hat = argmax_{i in [K]} p_i. Then the i-th block of g_x (i.e. the gradients corresponding to label i) is (g_x)_i = d/dW_i l_CE(f(x;theta), y_hat) = (p_i - I(y_hat = i)) z(x; V).
elements.pseudocode:
(g_x)_i = (p_i - I(y_hat == i)) * z, for i = 1..K
where p_i = softmax output for class i, y_hat = argmax(p), z = penultimate layer output.
The full gradient embedding g_x in R^{K*d} concatenates K blocks of d-dimensional vectors.

elements.name: Gradient norm lower bound (Proposition 1)
elements.description: The squared norm of the gradient w.r.t. last layer weights for any label y is ||g_x^y||^2 = (sum_i p_i^2 + 1 - 2*p_y) * ||z(x;V)||^2. This shows the hallucinated-label gradient y_hat is the minimizer of ||g_x^y|| over all y, making it a conservative (lower bound) estimate of gradient magnitude.
elements.source_text: For all y in {1, ..., K}, let g_x^y = d/dW l_CE(f(x; theta), y). Then ||g_x^y||^2 = (sum_{i=1}^K p_i^2 + 1 - 2*p_y) * ||z(x;V)||^2. Consequently, y_hat = argmin_{y in [K]} ||g_x^y||.
elements.pseudocode:
||g_x^{(y)}||^2 = (sum_i p_i^2 + 1 - 2*p_y) * ||z||^2
The hallucinated label y_hat = argmax(p_y) minimizes this over all y, so ||g_x^{(y_hat)}|| <= ||g_x^{(y)}|| for all y.

elements.name: Pairwise t-score for algorithm comparison
elements.description: Statistical test used to compare two algorithms across 5 repeated runs. mu_hat is the mean of per-run error differences, sigma_hat is the standard deviation. t = sqrt(5) * mu_hat / sigma_hat with critical value 2.776 (two-sided, p=0.05, df=4).
elements.source_text: For each (D,B,A,L) combination and each pair of algorithms (i,j), we have 5 test errors. We compute the t-score as t = sqrt(5) * mu_hat / sigma_hat, where mu_hat = (1/5) sum_{l=1}^5 (e_i^l - e_j^l), sigma_hat = sqrt((1/4) sum_{l=1}^5 (e_i^l - e_j^l - mu_hat)^2). We use the two-sided t-test: algorithm i beats algorithm j if t > 2.776.
elements.pseudocode:
mu_hat = mean(e_i^l - e_j^l for l in 1..5)
var_hat = (1/4) * sum((e_i^l - e_j^l - mu_hat)^2 for l in 1..5)
sigma_hat = sqrt(var_hat)
t = sqrt(5) * mu_hat / sigma_hat
# i beats j if t > 2.776; j beats i if t < -2.776

elements.name: Penalty matrix computation
elements.description: Aggregation of pairwise comparison results across label budgets. For each (D,B,A,L), if algorithm i beats j, penalize 1/n_{D,B,A} is added to P_{i,j}. Column averages show overall performance.
elements.source_text: For each (D,B,A) combination, suppose there are n_{D,B,A} different values of L. Then, for each L, if algorithm i beats algorithm j, we accumulate a penalty of 1/n_{D,B,A} to P_{i,j}; otherwise, if algorithm j beats algorithm i, we accumulate a penalty of 1/n_{D,B,A} to P_{j,i}.
elements.pseudocode:
P initialized to zeros.
For each (D,B,A) combination:
  n = number of L values for this (D,B,A)
  For each L:
    For each pair (i, j):
      if i beats j: P[i][j] += 1/n
      elif j beats i: P[j][i] += 1/n
# Column average is aggregate score (lower = better)

elements.name: Normalized error for CDF comparison
elements.description: Normalized error ne_i = e_bar_i / e_bar_r, where r is the index of the RAND baseline. CDFs are plotted comparing algorithms; higher CDF value at a given error means better performance.
elements.source_text: For each (D,B,A,L) combination, we compute the average error for each algorithm i as e_bar_i = (1/5) sum_{l=1}^5 e_l^l. To ensure that the errors of these algorithms are on the same scale, we compute the normalized error of every algorithm i, defined as ne_i = e_bar_i / e_bar_r, where r is the index of the RAND algorithm.
elements.pseudocode:
e_bar_i = mean(e_i^l for l in 1..5)
ne_i = e_bar_i / e_bar_rand
# Plot CDF of ne_i across all (D,B,A,L) combinations

elements.name: Label budget selection for comparisons
elements.description: The set of label budgets L used for fair comparison. n_0 is the smallest number of labels where RAND accuracy reaches 99% of its final accuracy. L = {M + 2^{m-1} * B : m in [floor(log((n_0 - M)/B))]}, giving exponentially spaced budgets.
elements.source_text: Specifically, we compute n_0, the smallest number of labels where RAND's accuracy reaches 99% of its final accuracy, and choose label budget L from {M + 2^{m-1} B : m in [floor(log((n_0-M)/B))]}.

elements.name: Binary logistic regression: hallucinated-label gradient
elements.description: Specialization of BADGE to binary logistic regression. The hallucinated-label gradient is g_hat_x = (1 - p_w(y_hat|x)) * (-y_hat * x).
elements.source_text: Now, given model w and example x, we define g_hat_x = d/dw l(w,(x,y_hat)) = (1-p_w(y_hat|x,theta)) * (-y_hat * x) as the loss gradient induced by the example with hallucinated label.
elements.pseudocode:
g_hat_x = (1 - sigmoid(y_hat * w . x)) * (-y_hat * x)
where y_hat = +1 if sigmoid(w . x) > 0.5, else -1

elements.name: Binary logistic loss
elements.description: The loss for binary logistic regression: l(w, (x,y)) = ln(1 + exp(-y * w . x)).
elements.source_text: The binary logistic loss of classifier w on example (x, y) is defined as: l(w, (x, y)) = ln(1 + exp(-yw . x)).
elements.pseudocode: l(w, (x, y)) = ln(1 + exp(-y * w . x))

elements.name: Hallucinated label (model's own prediction as proxy)
elements.description: The core idea behind BADGE: since the true label is unknown during active learning selection, use the model's own most likely prediction y_hat(x) = argmax_y f(x;theta)_y as a proxy label when computing gradients. This provides a computable gradient embedding that lower-bounds the gradient norm for any true label.
elements.source_text: As a proxy, we compute the gradient as if the model's current prediction on the example is the true label. We show in Proposition 1 that, assuming a common structure satisfied by most natural neural networks, the gradient norm with respect to the last layer using this label provides a lower bound on the gradient norm induced by any other label.

elements.name: Gradient embedding space
elements.description: The space of gradient embeddings {g_x : x in U} where each g_x encodes both the model's uncertainty about x (norm of g_x) and the direction of potential parameter update. K-MEANS++ operates in this space to select diverse, high-magnitude points.
elements.source_text: Since deep neural networks are optimized using gradient-based methods, we capture uncertainty about an example through the lens of gradients. In particular, we consider the model uncertain about an example if knowing the label induces a large gradient of the loss with respect to the model parameters and hence a large update to the model.

elements.name: Pool-based active learning setting
elements.description: The framework: the learner receives an unlabeled pool U and can request labels for any subset. The goal is to achieve low 0/1 error with minimal label queries.
elements.source_text: We consider the pool-based active learning setup, where the learner receives an unlabeled dataset U sampled according to D_X and can request labels sampled according to D_{Y|X} for any x in U. The goal of pool-based active learning is to find a classifier with a small expected 0/1 error using as few label queries as possible.

elements.name: Uncertainty via gradient magnitude
elements.description: A sample's uncertainty is measured by the norm of its gradient embedding. High-confidence samples have small gradient norms (p_i concentrated on one class), while uncertain samples have large norms.
elements.source_text: If the current model theta is highly confident about x, i.e. vector p is skewed towards a standard basis vector e_j, then y_hat = j, and vector (p_i - I(y_hat = i))_{i=1}^K has a small length. Therefore, g_x has a small length as well. Such high-confidence examples tend to have gradient embeddings of small magnitude, which are unlikely to be repeatedly selected by k-MEANS++.

elements.name: Diversity via k-MEANS++ sampling
elements.description: k-MEANS++ inherently trades off between magnitude and diversity: at small batch sizes it favors high-magnitude points (uncertainty), while at larger batch sizes it increasingly favors linearly independent / distant points (diversity). This replaces k-DPP, which has the same properties but higher computational cost.
elements.source_text: k-MEANS++ seeding selects centroids by iteratively sampling points in proportion to their squared distances from the nearest centroid that has already been chosen, which, like a k-DPP, tends to select a diverse batch of high-magnitude samples.

elements.name: Last-layer gradient restriction
elements.description: BADGE computes gradients only w.r.t. the last (output) layer parameters, not the entire network. This makes Proposition 1 tractable since the softmax + linear output has a simple analytical gradient.
elements.source_text: For all examples x in U \ S: Compute gradient embedding g_x = d/d(theta_out) l_CE(f(x;theta), y_hat(x))|_{theta=theta_t}, where theta_out refers to parameters of the final (output) layer.

elements.name: Classifier h_theta and scoring
elements.description: The classifier h_theta(x) = argmax_{y in [K]} f(x; theta)_y, where f(x; theta) in R^K is the probability vector. The classifier uses the network f parameterized by theta with fixed architecture.
elements.source_text: Our classifiers take the form h_theta(x) = argmax_{y in [K]} f(x; theta)_y, where f(x; theta) in R^K is a probability vector of scores assigned to candidate labels, given the example x and parameters theta.

elements.name: Softmax output layer parametrization
elements.description: The network f is parametrized by theta = (W, V) where W = [W_1; ...; W_K] in R^{K x d} are last-layer weights, and V are all previous layer weights. f(x; theta) = softmax(W . z(x; V)) where z is the penultimate layer output.
elements.source_text: Specifically, f is parametrized by theta = (W, V), where theta_out = W = (W_1, ..., W_K)^T in R^{K x d} are the weights of the last layer, and V consists of weights of all previous layers. This means that f(x;theta) = sigma(W . z(x;V)), where z is the nonlinear function that maps an input x to the output of the network's penultimate layer.

elements.name: k-MEANS++ vs k-DPP sampling comparison
elements.description: Comparison of k-MEANS++ and k-DPP sampling using gradient embeddings. Shows nearly identical accuracy but k-MEANS++ is substantially faster, especially at large batch sizes.
elements.source_text: Figure 1: Left and center: Learning curves for k-MEANS++ and k-DPP sampling with gradient embeddings for different scenarios. The performance of the two sampling approaches nearly perfectly overlaps. Right: A run time comparison (seconds) corresponding to the middle scenario.

elements.name: Batch diversity and gradient magnitude per method
elements.description: Compares four selection methods (k-DPP, k-MEANS++, Random, FF-k-CENTER) in terms of log Gram determinant (diversity) and average L2 norm (uncertainty). Shows k-MEANS++ achieves the best diversity and high magnitude.
elements.source_text: Figure 2: A comparison of batch selection algorithms using our gradient embedding. Left and center: Plots showing the log determinant of the Gram matrix of the selected batch of gradient embeddings as learning progresses. Right: The average embedding magnitude (a measurement of predictive uncertainty) in the selected batch.

elements.name: Active learning learning curves across baselines
elements.description: Main evaluation comparing BADGE against 6 baselines (CORESET, Confidence, Margin, Entropy, ALBL, Random) across 3 datasets (SVHN, CIFAR10, MNIST, 4 OpenML datasets), 3 architectures (MLP, ResNet, VGG), and 3 batch sizes (100, 1000, 10000). Total 231 experiments (7 methods x 11 dataset-arch pairs x 3 batch sizes).
elements.source_text: We evaluate our algorithms using three image datasets, SVHN, CIFAR10 and MNIST and four non-image datasets from the OpenML repository (#6, #155, #156, and #184). We study each situation with 7 active learning algorithms, including BADGE, making for 231 total experiments.

elements.name: Pairwise penalty matrix (Figure 4)
elements.description: Pairwise comparison of all 7 algorithms using t-test significance. Shows aggregate performance across all settings. BADGE column average is the lowest (best), indicating best overall performance.
elements.source_text: Figure 4: A pairwise penalty matrix over all experiments. Element P_{i,j} corresponds roughly to the number of times algorithm i outperforms algorithm j. Column-wise averages at the bottom show overall performance (lower is better).

elements.name: CDF of normalized errors (Figure 5)
elements.description: Cumulative distribution of normalized errors (relative to Random baseline) across all settings. Higher CDF value means better performance. BADGE shows the best overall CDF.
elements.source_text: Figure 5: The cumulative distribution function of normalized errors for all acquisition functions. We can see from Figure 5 that BADGE has the best overall performance.

elements.name: Gradient norm lower bound property
elements.description: The norm of the gradient embedding g_x (computed with the model's own prediction) is a lower bound on the gradient norm for any true label y. This guarantees the embedding conservatively estimates the example's potential influence on the model.
elements.source_text: Proposition 1. For all y in {1, ..., K}, let g_x^y = d/dW l_CE(f(x; theta), y). Then ||g_x^y||^2 = (sum_{i=1}^K p_i^2 + 1 - 2*p_y)*||z(x;V)||^2. Consequently, y_hat = argmin_{y in [K]} ||g_x^y||.

elements.name: Gradient norm captures model uncertainty
elements.description: When the model is highly confident (p concentrated on one class), the gradient embedding has small norm. When uncertain (p spread across classes), it has large norm. This means magnitude in gradient space = uncertainty.
elements.source_text: If the current model theta is highly confident about x, i.e. vector p is skewed towards a standard basis vector e_j, then y_hat = j, and vector (p_i - I(y_hat = i))_{i=1}^K has a small length. Therefore, g_x has a small length as well.

elements.name: k-DPP (Determinantal Point Process) sampling
elements.description: The theoretical ideal for batch selection: samples k points with probability proportional to the determinant of their Gram matrix. Naturally trades off quality (magnitude) and diversity (linear independence). Challenging to sample from efficiently for large batch sizes.
elements.source_text: A natural way of making this selection without introducing additional hyperparameters is to sample from a k-Determinantal Point Process (k-DPP). That is, to select a batch of k points with probability proportional to the determinant of their Gram matrix.

elements.name: Last layer gradient lower bound definition
elements.description: The uncertainty definition in BADGE -- gradient magnitude of the last layer with the hallucinated label -- guarantees some minimum update of parameters, as it lower-bounds the true gradient for any label.
elements.source_text: The definition of uncertainty (a lower bound on the gradient magnitude of the last layer) guarantees some update of parameters.

elements.name: Initial random set size M
elements.description: Number of examples drawn uniformly at random from U to initialize the labeled set. Set to M=100 in all experiments.
elements.source_text: We evaluate them in a batch-mode active learning setup with M=100 being the number of initial random labeled examples and batch size B varying from {100, 1000, 10000}.

elements.name: Batch size B
elements.description: Number of examples selected per active learning round. Evaluated at B in {100, 1000, 10000}.
elements.source_text: batch size B varying from {100, 1000, 10000}.

elements.name: Number of active learning iterations T
elements.description: Number of rounds of active learning selection. Each round selects B examples, so total queried is M + T*B.
elements.source_text: number of iterations T

elements.name: Training learning rate
elements.description: Learning rate used for model training. 0.001 for image datasets, 0.0001 for non-image (OpenML) datasets.
elements.source_text: We use a learning rate of 0.001 for image data and of 0.0001 for non-image data.

elements.name: Model architectures
elements.description: Three architectures used: two-layer MLP with ReLU (embedding dim 256 for image, 1024 for OpenML), 18-layer ResNet, 11-layer VGG. MNIST uses only MLP since it's too easy for CNNs.
elements.source_text: We consider three neural network architectures: a two-layer Perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP), an 18-layer convolutional ResNet, and an 11-layer VGG network.

elements.name: Training stopping criterion
elements.description: Models trained until training accuracy exceeds 99%. Using Adam optimizer with cross-entropy loss. No warm-starting and no data augmentation. All experiments repeated 5 times.
elements.source_text: We fit models using cross-entropy loss and the Adam variant of SGD until training accuracy exceeds 99%. We avoid warm starting and retrain models from scratch every time new samples are queried. All experiments are repeated five times. No learning rate schedules or data augmentation are used.

elements.name: k-MEANS++ diversity and convergence guarantee
elements.description: The randomization in k-MEANS++ guarantees that the selected centers approximate the k-means objective in expectation, ensuring diversity even for adversarially constructed datasets.
elements.source_text: The randomization associated with the k-MEANS++ initialization sampler implies that, even for adversarially constructed datasets, it eventually converges to a good solution. It is shown in (Arthur and Vassilvitskii) 2007) that the set of centers returned is guaranteed to approximate the k-means objective function in expectation, thus ensuring diversity.

elements.name: BADGE for binary logistic regression
elements.description: Analysis of BADGE in the special case of binary logistic regression (K=2, z(x;V)=x). Shows that when restricted to the decision boundary (w.x = 0), the hallucinated gradient equals the true gradient up to sign, making DPP sampling over hallucinated gradients equivalent to DPP over true gradients.
elements.source_text: Suppose that BADGE only selects examples from region S_w = {x : w . x = 0}, then as p_w(+1|x) = p_w(-1|x) = 1/2, we have that for all x in S_w, g_hat_x = s_x . g_x for some s_x in {+/- 1}. This implies that, sampling from a DPP induced by g_hat_x's is equivalent to sampling from a DPP induced by g_x's.
